strengths: Exploring uncertainty quantification and conformal prediction within the context of machine unlearning is an intriguing perspective.

The empirical evaluation includes a diverse set of unlearning algorithms (e.g., Retrain, Finetune, Random Label, GA, Teacher, Fisher Forgetting, SSD, NegGrad+, Salun) across multiple model architectures (ResNet-18 and ViT).
The paper includes extensive sensitivity experiments analyzing conformal prediction parameters across multiple target miscoverage levels $\alpha$.
weaknesses: Fundamental conceptual flaw regarding the goal of unlearning in random sample forgetting: The accepted standard for machine unlearning is to reproduce the distribution of a model retrained from scratch on $D_r$ (the Retrain baseline). In random instance forgetting, samples in $D_f$ come from the same data-generating distribution as the retain and test sets. Therefore, a properly retrained model (RT) will naturally achieve high accuracy on $D_f$ and contain the true label in its conformal prediction set with probability $1-\alpha$ (as confirmed in Table 4, where RT has 88.1% coverage on $D_f$ and 89.5% on $D_{test}$). The paper's 'Limit-Based Criterion' (seeking to minimize coverage and conformal ratio on $D_f$) conflates unlearning with adversarial scrubbing/targeted degradation. Forcing the model to exclude the ground truth of $D_f$ makes the model easily distinguishable from RT, which directly undermines privacy and differential-privacy-style guarantees.

Mathematical and derivation error in Eq. (8): In the standard C&W-style unlearning formulation (Eq. 7), the goal is to drive down the probability of the true label $p_t(x)$. However, the non-conformity score is defined as $S(x, y_t) = 1 - p_t(x)$, which is negatively correlated with $p_t(x)$. Directly substituting $S(x, y_t)$ for $p_t(x)$ in Eq. (8) gives $L_{unlearn}(x, y_t) = \max(S(x, y_t) - \bar{q}, -\Delta)$. Minimizing this expression pushes $S(x, y_t)$ down toward 0, which corresponds to pushing $p_t(x)$ toward 1. This contradicts the stated goal on page 6 of encouraging $\bar{q} - S(x, y_t) \ge \Delta$.

Heuristic and problematic metric definition: The Conformal Ratio is defined as $\text{CR} = \text{Coverage} / \text{Set Size}$. This ratio lacks formal statistical justification. In split conformal prediction, when prediction sets are empty (which frequently occurs when miscoverage $\alpha$ is elevated, as noted in Section 4.2), the set size can fall below 1, causing CR to exceed 1 (e.g., Table 4 and Table 5 show CR values such as 1.002 and 1.225). Conflating coverage and set size via a simple quotient does not provide a well-calibrated measure of predictive confidence or privacy.

Methodological inconsistency with the Retrain baseline in Table 7: The authors evaluate their unlearning framework on RT itself by setting $\lambda = 0.2$ and $\lambda = 0.5$. By definition, the Retrain model is trained only on the retained data $D_r$ without any knowledge of or optimization on $D_f$. Applying an adversarial unlearning penalty on $D_f$ to Retrain distorts the benchmark itself, creating an artificial model rather than the true gold standard.

strengths: The paper explores an interesting connection between uncertainty quantification via conformal prediction and the evaluation of machine unlearning.
The qualitative motivation using Grad-CAM visualizations provides an intuitive illustration of how misclassified forget samples can still retain salient class features.
The authors conduct evaluations across multiple unlearning baselines (e.g., Finetune, Random Label, GA, Fisher Forgetting, SSD, NegGrad+, Salun) on CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet.
weaknesses: Fundamental conceptual flaw regarding the objective of machine unlearning: In standard machine unlearning, the gold standard is the retrained model (RT), which is trained on the retain set $D_r$ from scratch without ever observing $D_f$. In random sample unlearning, $D_f$ is drawn i.i.d. from the underlying data distribution, so an RT model naturally generalizes to $D_f$ with high accuracy and standard conformal coverage (i.e., approximately $1-\alpha$, matching $D_{test}$). The paper posits under 'Criterion 2' that successful unlearning should minimize coverage and the Conformal Ratio (CR) on $D_f$. Forcing $D_f$ to be excluded from the prediction set confuses unlearning with adversarial targeted misclassification or 'anti-learning', pushing the model's behavior strictly away from the retrained baseline.

Methodological inconsistency in experiments: In Table 7, the authors apply their proposed unlearning framework to the Retrained model (RT) itself. A model retrained from scratch on $D_r$ has already completely excluded $D_f$; applying an unlearning loss to RT fundamentally contradicts the unlearning problem setup.

Ad-hoc definition and pathological behavior of Conformal Ratio (CR): The metric $\text{CR} = \text{Coverage} / \text{Set Size}$ lacks sound theoretical justification. When the model outputs high-entropy predictions across many classes (e.g., Fisher Forgetting in Table 4, where the set size inflates to 7.129 and test accuracy collapses to 41.1%), the set size expands dramatically, artificially driving CR down to 0.131. The authors interpret this as 'the highest forgetting quality', whereas it actually reflects catastrophic model degradation. Furthermore, when $\alpha=0.2$ and set sizes drop below 1.0 due to empty prediction sets, CR exceeds 1.0, exhibiting unstable and unintuitive behavior.

Misalignment in the MIA Conformal Metric: Defining ideal MIA unlearning as $\text{MIACR} = 1$ (forcing the prediction set to strictly be $\{0\}$) again misinterprets unlearning evaluation. A legitimate retrained model does not yield an MIA prediction of 0 with 100% confidence across all instances; rather, an unlearned model should match the MIA distribution of the retrained model.

Writing and presentation errors: The manuscript contains notable grammatical and phrasing errors (e.g., 'In addiction' in Section 6, inconsistent table references such as referencing Tiny ImageNet with ResNet-18 in Section B.2 while Table 12 uses ViT).

strengths: Exploring uncertainty quantification and set-valued predictions (via conformal prediction) to audit the residual influence of forgotten data is an interesting conceptual direction.

The empirical evaluation includes a wide range of established unlearning baselines (e.g., Retrain, Fine-tune, Random Label, Gradient Ascent, Fisher Forgetting, SSD, NegGrad+, Salun) across multiple confidence parameters.
weaknesses: Fundamental conceptual flaw regarding the objective of machine unlearning: In random data unlearning, the forget set D_f is sampled from the same data distribution as D_train and D_test. The gold standard of unlearning is retraining from scratch (RT), where D_f is unseen test data that naturally should achieve standard generalization accuracy and ~1-\alpha conformal coverage. The paper treats RT's non-zero coverage on D_f as a failure and advocates a 'Limit-Based Criterion' where CR(D_f) should be minimized toward 0. This promotes 'anti-learning' or adversarial data-poisoning rather than unlearning. This confusion is further underscored in Table 7, where the authors apply their unlearning framework directly to RT, which is conceptually unsound since RT never encountered the forget data.

Mathematical contradiction in the loss formulation: In Section 3, Eq. (1) defines the non-conformity score as S(x, y_i) = 1 - p_i(x). To remove the true label y_t from the conformal prediction set C(x) = {y_i : S(x, y_i) <= q}, one requires S(x, y_t) > q (i.e., driving S to be large and p_t to be small). However, Eq. (8) defines the unlearning loss as L_unlearn = max(S(x, y_t) - \bar{q}, -\Delta) and states that this loss is minimized. Minimizing S(x, y_t) - \bar{q} forces S(x, y_t) to become smaller, which drives p_t(x) closer to 1 and guarantees inclusion in the prediction set. The text even contradicts its own formula by stating it 'encourages \bar{q} - S(x, y_t) >= \Delta'. This represents a significant mathematical and typographical error in the core contribution.

Pathological behavior of the proposed Conformal Ratio (CR) metric: CR is defined as Coverage / Set Size. When a model's representations are severely corrupted (e.g., Fisher Forgetting in Table 4), the set size inflates dramatically (7.13 out of 10 classes), which artificially drives CR down to 0.131 and leads the paper to claim FF achieves the 'highest forgetting quality'. Furthermore, when Set Size is less than 1 (due to empty prediction sets at higher miscoverage rates \alpha), CR exceeds 1.0 (e.g., CR = 1.225 in Table 5), making it uncalibrated and difficult to interpret.

High calibration data requirements and violation of exchangeability: Split conformal prediction strictly relies on exchangeability between calibration data and evaluation data. In unlearning (especially class-wise forgetting or label perturbation as in RL), exchangeability is explicitly violated. The paper attempts to patch this with ad-hoc shadow models (Appendix B.4), which adds substantial computational overhead and undermines the distribution-free guarantees of conformal prediction. Furthermore, requiring a separate clean calibration set of 2,000 to 10,000 samples for unlearning is impractical in many privacy-critical settings.

Limited novelty of the optimization framework: Beyond the conformal threshold serving as an adaptive margin, the proposed unlearning objective essentially reduces to applying a Carlini-Wagner margin loss to suppress the target label on D_f, which is a standard adversarial forgetting baseline.

strengths: The paper explores an interesting connection between uncertainty quantification (specifically split conformal prediction) and machine unlearning.
The authors benchmark a wide range of existing machine unlearning methods (FT, RL, GA, Bad Teacher, SSD, NegGrad+, Salun, SFRon) across multiple configurations.
The proposed loss formulation combining conformal quantile thresholds with Carlini-Wagner style margins is a creative attempt to explicitly control prediction set membership.
weaknesses: Fundamental conceptual flaw regarding the definition of machine unlearning: In standard unlearning settings (especially random sample unlearning), the gold standard is retraining from scratch on the retain set (RT). Because forgotten samples $D_f$ are drawn i.i.d. from the same underlying data distribution as retain and test data, a truly unlearned model should generalize to $D_f$ just as it generalizes to unseen test data $D_{test}$. Consequently, a retrained model is expected to achieve accuracy on $D_f$ close to test accuracy, and its conformal prediction sets at confidence level $1-\alpha$ should cover the true label roughly $1-\alpha$ of the time (as confirmed by the authors' own Retrain results in Table 3: 94.1% coverage on $D_f$ vs 94.4% on $D_{test}$). Defining this coverage as 'fake unlearning' mischaracterizes standard generalization on exchangeable data as an unlearning failure.

The proposed mitigation actively induces over-forgetting and creates a new privacy leakage channel: Forcing the non-conformity score of $D_f$ above the conformal threshold $\bar{q}$ deliberately suppresses the true label so that $y_t \notin C(x)$. When a model achieves ~90% accuracy and 95% conformal coverage on unseen test data, but near 0% coverage on $D_f$, it behaves anomalies-specifically on $D_f$. An adversary performing membership inference or auditing can trivially recognize that a sample belonged to $D_f$ precisely because the model's conformal coverage on it is artificially suppressed compared to unseen data.

Self-contradictory evaluation criteria: The manuscript outlines two evaluation criteria in Section 2.3.1 (Gap to RT vs. Limit-Based Criterion), but fails to reconcile that they directly contradict each other. For random data forgetting, Retrain achieves a UA of only ~8.6% (i.e., ~91.4% accuracy on $D_f$). Under Criterion 2 ('higher UA / lower CR on $D_f$ is better'), methods that destroy performance on $D_f$ (e.g., UA > 30%) are praised, despite diverging significantly from RT under Criterion 1.

Severe presentation and formatting defects: Page 2 exhibits significant layout corruption, where line numbers (lines 37–68) are improperly rendered in the main text alongside duplicate versions of the same Grad-CAM figure/table ('Table 1' in the left column and 'Figure 1' in the right column) and duplicated body text. Typographical issues also appear throughout (e.g., 'In addiction' on page 10, 'CIFAT-10' in Table 2).

strengths: Exploring uncertainty quantification, and specifically conformal prediction, to inspect the residual information retained after machine unlearning is an interesting and timely direction.

The empirical evaluation tests a wide variety of unlearning baselines (Retrain, Finetune, Random Label, Gradient Ascent, Bad Teacher, Selective Synaptic Dampening, NegGrad+, Salun, and SFRon) across two vision benchmarks (CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet).
The appendix includes extensive ablation studies examining quantile stability, calibration set size, and varying miscoverage rates (alpha).
weaknesses: Fundamental conceptual flaw regarding the definition of unlearning: In standard machine unlearning (especially random instance forgetting), the gold standard is exact retraining from scratch on the retain set (RT). Because the forget set D_f is drawn from the same underlying distribution, an ideal retrained model should predict D_f with normal test-set accuracy, and a valid split conformal prediction set should cover the true label with probability roughly 1 - alpha (as observed for RT in Table 3 where coverage is ~0.94). Labeling this as 'fake unlearning' conflates machine unlearning with adversarial scrubbing or intentional misclassification of forget samples.

Contradictory evaluation criteria: The manuscript introduces two opposing criteria—Criterion 1 (Gap to RT) and Criterion 2 (Limit-based, minimizing CR on D_f). Under Criterion 2, driving CR(D_f) to zero actively diverges from RT. In fact, applying the proposed CPU loss to RT itself (CPU-RT in Table 5 and Table 14) causes the model's UA to increase from 8.6% to 17.7%, meaning the method penalizes and alters the behavior of the ground-truth retrained model. This circular logic undermines the validity of the proposed evaluation methodology.

Over-engineered formulation for a simple objective: Despite being introduced as a novel integration of conformal prediction and Carlini-Wagner adversarial loss, Eq. 9 simplifies directly: since S(x, y_t) = 1 - p_t(x), the loss is L_unlearn = max{p_t(x) - (1 - \bar{q}), -\Delta}. This is simply a standard margin penalty pushing down the ground-truth softmax probability p_t(x) below a threshold 1 - \bar{q}. Such deliberate over-suppression of probabilities for D_f creates out-of-distribution artifacts that can paradoxically make forget samples easier to detect via auditing.

Severe presentation and manuscript formatting issues: Page 2 exhibits broken LaTeX compilation where raw line numbers (lines 37–68), an incomplete/duplicated Table 1, and Figure 1 are jumbled together with overlapping text. In addition, the text skips from question (Q2) on page 4 to (Q4) on page 6 with no (Q3), and contains typos such as 'In addiction' (Section 6), 'CIFAT-10' (Table 2 caption), and missing citation years ('Tailor et al.').

Evaluation lacks state-of-the-art privacy attacks: Unlearning evaluation relies on standard threshold MIA rather than modern, rigorous membership inference audits (such as Likelihood Ratio Attacks / LiRA or Canary insertions), which are crucial to determine whether the proposed framework truly eliminates data leakage or merely introduces distribution distortions.

strengths: The paper introduces an interesting perspective by connecting conformal prediction and uncertainty quantification to the evaluation of machine unlearning, highlighting that simple top-1 misclassification can mask high residual confidence.
The empirical evaluation is extensive, comparing 9 baseline unlearning algorithms across standard vision benchmarks (CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18, and Tiny ImageNet with ViT).

The analysis of 'fake unlearning' through prediction set coverage and Grad-CAM visualizations provides intuitive evidence that standard classification accuracy alone does not capture the full predictive distribution.
weaknesses: Fundamental conceptual flaw in defining unlearning goals: In random sample unlearning (which forms the bulk of the experimental evaluation), the gold standard is Retraining from scratch (RT). Since forget data $D_f$ is drawn i.i.d. from the underlying data distribution, an ideal retrained model should treat $D_f$ exactly like unseen test data $D_{test}$ (achieving high accuracy and valid conformal coverage on $D_f$). Pushing the true label completely out of the prediction set on $D_f$ via the proposed loss (Eq. 9) amounts to adversarial scrubbing/suppression rather than true unlearning, causing the model to diverge further from the retrained baseline.

Ambiguity and questionable formulation of the Conformal Ratio (CR) metric: The metric $CR = \text{Coverage} / \text{Set Size}$ exhibits pathological properties. For example, a completely uninformative model that produces trivial prediction sets covering all classes ($|C(x)| = K$) achieves a very low CR ($1/K$), which according to the paper's 'Limit-Based Criterion' is rewarded as 'stronger unlearning'. This conflates uncertainty/unusefulness with effective forgetting.

Data requirements and calibration assumptions: The approach requires setting aside substantial separate held-out calibration sets ($D_c$ for evaluation and $D_c'$ for the unlearning optimization loop). In real-world unlearning scenarios with constrained data, carving out multiple clean calibration subsets is non-trivial and may degrade retain set training.

Writing and presentation issues: There are several typos and editorial errors throughout the text (e.g., 'CIFAT-10' in Table 2 caption, referencing Table 1 instead of Figure 1 on page 2, and 'In addiction' in Section 6).
